# Diagnosing Persistent Rear Clanging on a Mazda 3

Replacing suspension components often yields immediate results, but residual noise after an installation can point to secondary issues or installation errors. In your case, the transition from a broken rear spring to loose sway bar links provided relief, yet a specific "clanging" sound persists over major bumps. This behavior suggests that while the primary isolation points have been addressed, there may be remaining play in the anti-roll system geometry or a different shock absorber mounting issue entirely.

The fact that you successfully eliminated the noise associated with minor imperfections indicates the sway bar links were indeed the culprit for those specific inputs. However, the persistence of the sound over sharp inclines and speed bumps implies excessive lateral movement or a failure in another connection point. When installing sway bar end links without removing the torsion spring (the sway bar itself), you introduce geometric constraints. Flexing the new link into position against a rigid bar can sometimes result in improper alignment or uneven preload on the bushings, even if the fasteners feel tight.

Regarding your concern about the passenger-side link appearing at an odd angle: visual inspection of suspension geometry is notoriously difficult without proper lighting and vehicle elevation. A sway bar link should generally appear straight relative to the lower control arm when the vehicle is unloaded and sitting level. If one side looks crooked compared to the other, it usually indicates that the bar was twisted during installation or that a bushing is worn enough to allow significant articulation. While nylon lock nuts are designed to retain torque, they do not prevent thread galling if over-torqued or vibrated against repeatedly. The best practice is to remove them, clean any debris from the threads, and reinstall with a standard wrench before applying final torque and breaking in the lock washer.

A critical diagnostic step for remaining clanging noises after link replacement is checking the sway bar bushings themselves. If the rubber isolators inside the mounting bracket are cracked or separated, metal-to-metal contact will occur exactly when you hit a large bump, creating that distinct metallic clang. This issue can coexist with bad links; once the loose links are secured, the vibration frequency changes enough to make the failing bushing audible again. Inspect the brackets where the bar passes through the frame or subframe for signs of cracking rubber or exposed metal shavings.

Another possibility is the rear shock absorber mounting bolts. Over 100,000 miles, these can stretch or strip their threads in the control arm or unibody, leading to a rattle that mimics suspension clanging. Verify that all four shock mounts are torqued to factory specifications and that the washers behind them are not flattened. If you have access to a torque wrench, re-torque the sway bar end link nuts after driving 50–100 miles; vibration can settle components in their seats, altering clearance slightly.

If the bushings and links check out correctly, the noise might originate from the rear trailing arm bushings or even the differential pinion support bearing, though these are less common sources of intermittent clanging unless severe damage has occurred. Systematically isolating each component by having a helper bounce the vehicle while you listen closely to specific locations will help narrow down whether the sound is lateral (sway bar) or vertical (shocks/struts).
